finding.claim: reset_password_loose uses PHP loose == to compare the stored reset token with the submitted token. A boolean true submitted as the token matches any non-empty stored token, and numeric-looking tokens match alternate numeric spellings, so the password can be overwritten without knowing the token.
finding.source: $token parameter of reset_password_loose (line 2). Its origin is outside this repository; if the caller passes an unvalidated JSON value, the attacker controls its type and value.
finding.sink: Password overwrite: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... (reset.php:5-6)

trace.note: Fetches the stored token for $email with $db->query(...)->fetch(), quoting $email via $db->quote()
if ($row && $row['token'] == $token): loose comparison; true == non-empty string is true, and numeric strings compare numerically
UPDATE users SET pw = password_hash($new) executes when the comparison passes
Returns true to the caller, signalling a successful reset

finding.guards_checked: $db->quote() on $email at lines 3 and 6 prevents SQL injection through the email. No type check on $token, no expiry check, and no caller-side validation visible in the repository. The comparison is also not constant-time. Exploitability depends on the caller passing a non-string token, which could not be verified.

verdict.guard_found: No type check or validation on $token anywhere in the repo. $db->quote() on $email (reset.php:3, 5-6) blocks SQL injection through the email only. The sibling reset_password (reset.php:14) uses hash_equals with (string)$token, a stricter check, but it is a different function and does not guard reset_password_loose.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: the loose `==` at reset.php:4 gates the password UPDATE at reset.php:5-6, and reset.php:7 returns true. The repo is a single file with no caller of reset_password_loose, so whether an attacker can supply a boolean or otherwise non-string $token cannot be determined from the code available, which the candidate itself concedes.

finding.claim: Reset tokens are not single-use and no expiry is checked in either function. After a successful reset the resets row is never deleted or invalidated, so the same token can reset the password again later. fetch() returns only one unordered row, so when several reset requests exist for an email, only an arbitrary row is checked and stale tokens can remain valid.
finding.source: Any holder of a previously issued reset token (for example one leaked via email, logs, a referrer, or a shared device). The token is supplied through the $token parameter of reset_password_loose (line 2) and reset_password (line 12).
finding.sink: Password overwrite: UPDATE users SET pw = ... (reset.php:5-6 and 15-16)

trace.note: Fetches a single row from resets for $email with fetch(); no ORDER BY, no timestamp or expiry filter
Compares the stored token with the submitted token (loose comparison in this function)
Returns true; no DELETE or UPDATE of the resets row exists anywhere in this file, so the token stays valid
reset_password repeats the same single-row fetch, with the same lack of expiry and single-use controls
reset_password returns true or false with no invalidation step

finding.guards_checked: No expiry or timestamp check, no single-use invalidation, and no ordering on the fetch query in this file. The caller or a scheduled job may delete or expire rows, but nothing in the repository shows that. Logic flaw confirmed within this file; severity depends on the caller's cleanup.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:3 and :13 run a bare SELECT with no expiry, timestamp, or ORDER BY filter. reset.php:4 uses loose == and :14 uses hash_equals, but both only compare the token. Neither function deletes or updates the resets row after success (:7, :17 return true directly). The repository contains only reset.php, so no cleanup job or caller-side invalidation is visible.
verdict.reason: reset.php:5-7 and :15-17 overwrite the password and return true without invalidating the resets row, and reset.php:3 and :13 apply no expiry check, so a previously issued token stays valid for a later reset. The attacker needs prior possession of the token, so severity depends on token exposure and on any cleanup outside this file, but the logic flaw is real and nothing in the repo blocks it.

finding.claim: reset_password's hash_equals() call can return true when the stored token is NULL or empty and the submitted token is null, omitted or empty, because both sides coerce to the empty string. The loose comparison in reset_password_loose behaves the same way through null == "".
finding.source: $token parameter of reset_password (line 12), which can be null or an empty string when supplied by an attacker. The stored value comes from the resets table, whose schema is not in the repository.
finding.sink: Password overwrite: UPDATE users SET pw = ... (reset.php:15-16)

trace.note: Fetches $row['token'] for $email; a NULL column value is possible if the schema allows it
hash_equals($row['token'], (string)$token): NULL coerces to "" and (string)null is "", so equal values compare true
UPDATE users SET pw = password_hash($new) executes when the comparison passes

finding.guards_checked: The (string) cast does not reject empty values, and nothing in the file checks for an empty or null token. Whether the resets.token column can be NULL or empty is not verifiable from the repository, so this is plausible rather than confirmed.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:14 has no empty or null check on $row['token'] or $token; the (string) cast only normalizes null to "". reset.php:4 has no such check either. Only a `$row &&` truthiness check exists, and it passes for a row whose token is "" or NULL.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: at reset.php:14, hash_equals("", "") returns true when the stored token is NULL or "" and the submitted token is null, omitted or "", and no guard in the file blocks that, but whether an attacker can reach it depends on whether the resets table ever holds a NULL or empty token for an email, and neither the schema nor the reset-creation code is in the repository (reset.php:13 only reads it).
